# nish/crypto/aes

AES-128 and AES-256 (FIPS 197), GCM on top of them (NIST SP 800-38D), and QUIC's AES header-protection mask (RFC 9001 §5.4.3).

```ts
import {
  AES_BLOCK,
  AES_GCM_TAG_SIZE,
  AesKey,
  aesBitslicedRound,
  aesEncryptBlock,
  aesGcmOpen,
  aesGcmSeal,
  aesGcmTagMask,
  aesHeaderMask,
  aesKey,
  aesKeyInto,
  aesKeyWipe,
  ghashMultiply,
} from "nish/crypto/aes";
```

<scalar-code-group>

```ts example.ts
import { aesKey, aesGcmSeal, aesGcmOpen, aesKeyWipe } from "nish/crypto/aes";

const key = aesKey(keyBytes); // 16 or 32 bytes, else null
if (key !== null) {
  // never seal two messages under one key with the same IV
  const sealed: u8[] | null = aesGcmSeal(key, iv, aad, plaintext);
  const opened: u8[] | null = sealed === null ? null : aesGcmOpen(key, iv, aad, sealed);
  aesKeyWipe(key);
}
```

</scalar-code-group>

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="aes​Encrypt​Block" icon="phosphor/regular/function" href="#aesencryptblock">

</scalar-card>

GCM authenticated decryption (SP 800-38D §7.2): `sealed` is the ciphertext followed by its 16-byte tag, and the answer is the plaintext, or `null` when the tag does not verify, the IV is empty, `sealed` is shorter than a tag or the key is not one `aesKey` made.

</scalar-card>

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="aes​Gcm​Tag​Mask" icon="phosphor/regular/function" href="#aesgcmtagmask">

All-ones when the tag `tagHi:tagLo` equals `gotHi:gotLo`, zero otherwise: the difference of both halves ORed into one word and handed to `ctEq`, so every bit of both tags is read and nothing is branched on until the caller tests the one answer.

</scalar-card>

`aesKey` into an `AesKey` the caller already holds: the key schedule of a 16-byte (AES-128) or 32-byte (AES-256) `key`, bitsliced, and H = E(K, 0^128) for GCM, written into `out`, whose `roundKeys` must already be the `8 * (rounds + 1)` words that key length needs (88 or 120).

<scalar-callout type="info">

Written from the specifications and the papers below, in this module's own
layout, with one exception: `ghashMul32` is adapted from BearSSL's
`bmul64`, and carries BearSSL's notice. Nothing else here is ported from
another implementation.

</scalar-callout>

- **Bitslicing** is the idea of E. Käsper and P. Schwabe, "Faster and
  Timing-Attack Resistant AES-GCM" (CHES 2009): hold bit `b` of many bytes
  in one word, so that SubBytes is a Boolean circuit run on whole words and
  no byte ever becomes a table index.
- **The S-box circuit** is J. Boyar and R. Peralta's, "A depth-16 circuit
  for the AES S-box" (SEC 2012) and the 113-gate listing published with it:
  a linear layer in, 32 ANDs over GF(2^4) and GF(2^2) arithmetic, a linear
  layer out. `aesSbox` keeps their variable names so it can be read against
  the paper, gate by gate.
- **GHASH's multiply** is carry-less multiplication done with the integer
  multiplier, by leaving three zero bits of "holes" between the bits of each
  operand so that the carries of an integer product land where nothing is
  read — T. Pornin's technique, and `ghashMul32` is his `bmul64` from
  BearSSL narrowed to 32-bit operands — with Karatsuba's three-for-four
  split on top (this module's own), and the
  reduction of S. Gueron and M. Kounavis, "Intel Carry-Less Multiplication
  Instruction and its Usage for Computing the GCM Mode" (2010), for GCM's
  bit-reflected field.

<scalar-detail title="The bitsliced state">

Four blocks at a time sit in eight `u64` words,
`q[0..7]`, word `b` holding bit `b` of all 64 bytes. Inside a word, block `k`
owns the 16 bits from `16k`, and in those the byte in row `r` and column `c`
of the AES state is bit `4r + c`: each row is one nibble. That makes the two
permutations cheap.

ShiftRows turns row `r` by `r` columns, which is a rotation of nibble `r` by
`r` bits; MixColumns needs each byte's neighbour in the next row of its
column, which is the word rotated by four bits inside each 16-bit lane.
Getting 64 bytes in and out of that layout is an 8 × 8 bit-matrix transpose
per byte lane (`aesTranspose`, three rounds of masked swaps between words)
after placing each byte in the word and slot the transpose will carry to its
bit (`aesPack`, `aesUnpack`).

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Constant time">

No table is read anywhere, key schedule included: the
S-box is the circuit, and `SubWord` in the key schedule runs the same circuit
on a four-byte state. No branch or index depends on a key, a plaintext, a tag
or H: every `if` and every loop bound is on a length, a block number or the
round count.

GHASH multiplies with no table and no data-dependent shift, and `aesGcmOpen`
computes the whole tag and compares it with `aesGcmTagMask` — a difference
ORed into one word and handed to `ctEq` — before it decrypts or returns
anything. What `tests/ct-asm.js` verifies by disassembly on x86-64 and
aarch64 is one full round (`aesBitslicedRound`: S-box circuit, ShiftRows,
MixColumns, AddRoundKey), one GHASH multiply (`ghashMultiply`) and the tag
compare (`aesGcmTagMask`).

A golden case compiles to one module and cannot import this one, so
`tests/cases/ct_asm_aes` holds a verbatim copy of those three and the helpers
they call, and `tests/link/crypto_aes` checks that the copy and this module
agree on generated inputs, so neither can drift from the other unnoticed.
Everything around them — packing bytes, the key schedule, the loops over
blocks — is the discipline above and not a verified property.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="The seams">

Four private functions do nearly all of the cipher's work,
each called from exactly one place: `aesScheduleInto` (the key schedule),
`aesBlockInto` (one block), `aesCtrInto` (GCTR over a run of bytes) and
`ghashBlocksInto` (GHASH over a run of bytes). Each takes the arrays its
caller passes, writes into them and allocates nothing the caller needs back,
and its one caller checks every precondition it names first.

That is what lets the compiler, natively, put each of those four calls behind
a branch on the runtime's `nish_aes_hw` (`src/kernels.ts`, lowered in
`src/emit.ts`): on a CPU with AES-NI and PCLMULQDQ, or the ARMv8 AES and
PMULL instructions, the call goes to a kernel in `runtime/runtime-aes.c` that
does no bounds checks of its own; on any other CPU, under `NISH_AES=soft`, on
wasm32 and under Node, the body here runs (WP38 S5, `docs/wp38-simd.md`). The
bodies are the bitsliced code, and keep their own defensive checks. The
kernel keeps its own layout in a key's `roundKeys`, which a process only ever
reads under the one answer `nish_aes_hw` gives it.

</scalar-detail>

What runs outside the seams, and so on the bitsliced code whichever way
they go: `ghashLengths`, the last GHASH block of every tag, and so the end
of J0's derivation for an IV that is not 12 bytes, multiplies with
`ghashMultiply` on the state a seam left; and `aesGcmTag` folds E(K, J0)
into it. A kernel therefore leaves the GHASH state in this module's own
form, two big-endian words, and `tests/link/crypto_aes_agree` holds the two
paths to the same bytes on the IVs that take that road.

<scalar-callout type="warning">

**What is refused.** A key of any length but 16 or 32 bytes (AES-192 is out
of scope), a block or a sample that is not 16 bytes, an empty IV (SP 800-38D
§5.2.1.1 asks for at least one bit), a sealed input shorter than its tag, a
plaintext too long for its sealed form to be an array, and an `AesKey`
`aesKey` did not make answer `null`; so does a tag that does not verify. An
IV of any other non-zero length is hashed into the first counter block as
§7.1 says.

</scalar-callout>

Private names carry the `aes` / `ghash` prefix because a `std/` module's
private functions share the importing program's flat symbol namespace
(`docs/wp26-stdlib.md` §3e).

## Functions

### aesBitslicedRound

One full middle round of the cipher on bitsliced state — SubBytes,
ShiftRows, MixColumns, then the round key of eight words from `at` — for
four blocks at once. Straight-line code with no branch and no index but
`at`, which is a round number times eight. Exported so that
`tests/link/crypto_aes` can hold the copy the disassembly check reads to
this one; a caller has no other use for it.

```ts
function aesBitslicedRound(
  q: u64[],
  rk: u64[],
  at: i32,
): void
```

<scalar-field name="q" type="u64[]" required>

The bitsliced state of four blocks, eight words, updated in place.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="rk" type="u64[]" required>

The bitsliced round keys.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="at" type="i32" required>

Where this round's eight words start in `rk`.

</scalar-field>

### aesEncryptBlock

One block encrypted (FIPS 197 §5.1, ECB): 16 bytes in, 16 fresh bytes out, or
`null` for another length.

```ts
function aesEncryptBlock(
  key: AesKey,
  block: u8[],
): u8[] | null
```

<scalar-field name="key" type="AesKey" required>

The expanded key.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="block" type="u8[]" required>

The 16 bytes to encrypt; it is read, not kept.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="u8[] | null">

A fresh 16-byte block, or `null` for another length or a key
  `aesKey` would not make.

</scalar-field>

### aesGcmOpen

GCM authenticated decryption (SP 800-38D §7.2): `sealed` is the ciphertext
followed by its 16-byte tag, and the answer is the plaintext, or `null` when
the tag does not verify, the IV is empty, `sealed` is shorter than a tag or
the key is not one `aesKey` made.
The tag is computed over the received ciphertext and compared in constant
time before anything is decrypted, so a forgery yields no plaintext at all.

```ts
function aesGcmOpen(
  key: AesKey,
  iv: u8[],
  aad: u8[],
  sealed: u8[],
): u8[] | null
```

<scalar-field name="key" type="AesKey" required>

The expanded key.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="iv" type="u8[]" required>

The nonce the message was sealed with.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="aad" type="u8[]" required>

The data authenticated with it; must match what was sealed.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="sealed" type="u8[]" required>

The ciphertext followed by its 16-byte tag.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="u8[] | null">

A fresh array holding the plaintext, or `null` if the tag fails or
  the input is bad.

</scalar-field>

### aesGcmSeal

GCM authenticated encryption (SP 800-38D §7.1): the ciphertext followed by
the 16-byte tag, in one fresh array. The IV may be any non-zero length; 12
bytes is the fast and usual one. `null` for an empty IV, for a key
`aesKey` did not make, and for a plaintext longer than 2^31 - 17 bytes,
whose sealed form would not fit in an array.

```ts
function aesGcmSeal(
  key: AesKey,
  iv: u8[],
  aad: u8[],
  plaintext: u8[],
): u8[] | null
```

<scalar-field name="key" type="AesKey" required>

The expanded key.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="iv" type="u8[]" required>

The nonce, any non-zero length; it must never repeat under one key.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="aad" type="u8[]" required>

Data authenticated but not encrypted; may be empty.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="plaintext" type="u8[]" required>

The message to encrypt; it is read, not kept.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="u8[] | null">

A fresh array of ciphertext then tag, `plaintext.length + 16` bytes,
  or `null` for bad input.

</scalar-field>

### aesGcmTagMask

All-ones when the tag `tagHi:tagLo` equals `gotHi:gotLo`, zero otherwise:
the difference of both halves ORed into one word and handed to `ctEq`, so
every bit of both tags is read and nothing is branched on until the caller
tests the one answer. Exported, like `aesBitslicedRound`, so the
disassembly check's copy can be held to it.

```ts
function aesGcmTagMask(
  tagHi: u64,
  tagLo: u64,
  gotHi: u64,
  gotLo: u64,
): u64
```

<scalar-field name="tagHi" type="u64" required>

The high half of the expected tag.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="tagLo" type="u64" required>

The low half of the expected tag.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="gotHi" type="u64" required>

The high half of the received tag.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="gotLo" type="u64" required>

The low half of the received tag.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="u64">

All-ones if the tags match, zero if they do not.

</scalar-field>

### aesHeaderMask

The AES header-protection mask of RFC 9001 §5.4.3: the first five bytes of
the 16-byte `sample` encrypted under the header-protection key. `null` for
a sample of another length.

```ts
function aesHeaderMask(
  key: AesKey,
  sample: u8[],
): u8[] | null
```

<scalar-field name="key" type="AesKey" required>

The header-protection key.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="sample" type="u8[]" required>

The 16 bytes sampled from the packet's ciphertext.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="u8[] | null">

A fresh 5-byte mask, or `null` for another sample length or a key
  `aesKey` would not make.

</scalar-field>

### aesKey

Makes an `AesKey` from 16 bytes (AES-128) or 32 (AES-256): the key
schedule, bitsliced, and H = E(K, 0^128) for GCM. Any other length — 24
bytes included, since AES-192 is not offered — answers `null`.

```ts
function aesKey(key: u8[]): AesKey | null
```

<scalar-field name="key" type="u8[]" required>

The raw key, 16 or 32 bytes; it is read, not kept, and the caller
  still wipes it.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="AesKey | null">

A fresh key, which the caller hands to `aesKeyWipe` when done, or
  `null` for another length.

</scalar-field>

### aesKeyInto

`aesKey` into an `AesKey` the caller already holds: the key schedule of a
16-byte (AES-128) or 32-byte (AES-256) `key`, bitsliced, and H = E(K,
0^128) for GCM, written into `out`, whose `roundKeys` must already be the
`8 * (rounds + 1)` words that key length needs (88 or 120). It answers
whether it did; a key of another length, or a schedule array of the wrong
size for it (or an `h` that is not two words), answers `false` and leaves
`out` as it was.

`aesKey` makes a fresh `AesKey` and stores its schedule into it, which no
arena scope may be put around; this stores numbers only, so a caller that
keeps one `AesKey` per connection installs every key inside a `using a =
arena()` block and leaves the arena where it was. The schedule and H are
secret: the caller hands `out` to `aesKeyWipe` when it is done with the key.

The schedule is written straight into `out.roundKeys`, and the working copies
the bitsliced schedule and the block H passes through are wiped with `wipe`'s
volatile stores before they are released. On a CPU that runs the runtime's
kernels (the seams, in the module docs) those copies are the kernels' own, in
`runtime/runtime-aes.c`, and what they leave in vector registers no wipe here
reaches.

`aesKey` makes its key through this, so this is the one call of
`aesScheduleInto`, and the checks its contract needs are made here.

```ts
function aesKeyInto(
  key: u8[],
  out: AesKey,
): boolean
```

<scalar-field name="key" type="u8[]" required>

The raw key, 16 or 32 bytes; it is read, not kept, and the caller
  still wipes it.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="out" type="AesKey" required>

The key to overwrite, its `roundKeys` sized for this key length.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="boolean">

`true` if `out` now holds the key; `false` if it was left as it was.

</scalar-field>

### aesKeyWipe

Zeroes everything secret `key` holds — every word of `roundKeys`, the
runtime kernels' powers of H after the schedule included, and `h` — with
`wipe`'s volatile stores, which no optimiser removes however dead the key
is about to be. `rounds` is not secret and stays. A wiped key seals under
an all-zero schedule and, its H being zero, opens nothing (`aesGcmOpen`);
`aesKeyInto` installs a new key into it.

```ts
function aesKeyWipe(key: AesKey): void
```

<scalar-field name="key" type="AesKey" required>

The key to wipe; it stays usable as an `aesKeyInto` target.

</scalar-field>

### ghashMultiply

GHASH's multiply (SP 800-38D §6.3), `y = y · H` in GF(2^128), with `y` as
two words `y[0]` (high) and `y[1]` (low) of the block read big-endian and
H likewise in `hHi` and `hLo`.

GCM numbers a block's bits from the first, so the block read big-endian is
the polynomial with its coefficients reversed. The carry-less product of
two reversed polynomials is the reversed product one bit short, so the
256-bit product is shifted left once, and then its low half — the
coefficients of x^128 and up — is folded into the high half by
x^128 = x^7 + x^2 + x + 1, in two steps because the fold of the lowest
seven bits lands back in the low half (Gueron and Kounavis, §4 of the
paper cited in the header).

The 128 × 128 product is Karatsuba twice over: three 64 × 64 products, each
of three 32 × 32 ones from `ghashMul32`. Straight-line code; exported, like
`aesBitslicedRound`, so the disassembly check's copy can be held to it.

```ts
function ghashMultiply(
  y: u64[],
  hHi: u64,
  hLo: u64,
): void
```

<scalar-field name="y" type="u64[]" required>

The running GHASH value, two words, multiplied in place.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="hHi" type="u64" required>

The high half of H.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="hLo" type="u64" required>

The low half of H.

</scalar-field>

## Classes

### AesKey

An AES key, expanded: the round keys already bitsliced, and GCM's hash key
H = E(K, 0^128), so a key used for many messages is expanded once.

Make one with `aesKey`. The constructor and the fields are public only
because tests build keys by hand and read their words, and a key built or
edited by hand is not trusted: one whose shape is not what `aesKey` makes
answers `null` everywhere (`aesKeyUsable`), and one whose H is zero opens
nothing (`aesGcmOpen`). On the runtime kernels' path GHASH takes H and its
powers from `roundKeys`, while `ghashLengths` and a non-12-byte IV's J0 take
it from `h`; `aesKey` writes both from one schedule, so they agree. A key
edited so that they disagree is outside the contract, and what it seals then
depends on which path the process runs.

Both are secret. A holder done with a key hands it to `aesKeyWipe`, whose
volatile stores zero all of `roundKeys` (the kernels' tail of H's powers
included) and `h`, and stand however dead the key is about to be.

```ts
class AesKey
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new AesKey(rounds: i32, roundKeys: u64[])` | Wraps a schedule array and allocates `h`; neither is filled. `aesKey` calls this and then fills both, and a caller makes keys with `aesKey`. |
| `h: u64[]` | H as a big-endian 128-bit number, two words: `h[0]` the high half and `h[1]` the low. An array rather than two scalar fields, so that `aesKeyWipe`'s volatile wipe reaches it. |
| `roundKeys: u64[]` | Round key `i` in the bitsliced layout, replicated into all four block lanes, as eight words from `8 * i`: `8 * (rounds + 1)` words in all. In a native process that runs the runtime's AES kernels (the seams, above), the same words hold the kernels' layout instead, `runtime/runtime-aes.c`'s. |
| `rounds: i32` | Nr: 10 for AES-128, 14 for AES-256. |
